data.question: Should block_k be lowered from 3 to 2, so that parked robots are evicted sooner, even though companies B and C voted against it? Adopting it would require a human-approved override or revision of the regulation's voting and quorum rule, so the alternative is to keep the current rules (v1).
data.background: Amendment 1 passed cadl check and the constitution and improved the main goal on_time_deliveries by +9.2 on 5/5 seeds. B and C voted it down, so it cannot be adopted as an ordinary rule change. Getting past their votes means changing how the regulation counts votes or applying an override, and that is a regulation-layer decision. The constitution reserves those decisions for humans, and the trade-off between customers and the companies' own utility is not mine to settle.

options.summary: Adopt block_k 3 → 2. Measured results: on-time rises from 121.8 to 131.0 (+9.2, 5/5 seeds improved). Late falls from 10.4 to 1.2. Blocked s falls from 2404 to 985. Lowest on-time rate rises from 0.84 to 0.98, and unfinished stays at 0.0. Road violations rise from 25.8 to 34.0. Utility A / B / C moves from 38.4 / 38.9 / 28.8 to 45.4 / 37.2 / 19.0. Because B and C voted ×, adoption needs a human override or a regulation revision of the vote and quorum rule.
options.stakeholders: Customers of all three companies gain: more orders arrive within the promised time, and the weakest company's on-time rate rises to 0.98. Company A gains utility (38.4 → 45.4). Company B loses a little (38.9 → 37.2). Company C loses heavily (28.8 → 19.0), likely because its robots are evicted from parking spots more often. Other road users bear more road violations (25.8 → 34.0). Overriding B's and C's votes also weakens the companies' trust in the voting process and sets a precedent.

options.summary: Make no change and stay at v1. On-time stays at 121.8, late at 10.4, blocked s at 2404, and lowest on-time rate at 0.84. Road violations stay at 25.8, and utility A / B / C stays at 38.4 / 38.9 / 28.8. The vote and quorum rule is left untouched.
options.stakeholders: Companies B and C keep their current utility, and C is spared a large loss. The voting process is respected. Customers lose the measured gain: about 9 more late deliveries per period, and the weakest company's customers stay at a 0.84 on-time rate. Company A forgoes its gain.

recommendation.reason: The KPI ranks town-wide on-time delivery first and then asks that no company's customers be left behind. Option 1 improves both: +9.2 on-time on 5/5 seeds, and the lowest on-time rate rises from 0.84 to 0.98. The KPI also explicitly allows a regulation revision when votes block amendments that are good for customers. Two costs remain: road violations rise from 25.8 to 34.0, and C's utility drops sharply. I therefore suggest adopting it with an explicit record of the override. I also suggest the human consider compensating C or reviewing the change in a later period, and confirm that the higher road-violation count is acceptable.
assumptions: The 5-seed measurement represents normal demand in the coming periods.
C's utility loss falls on the company and not on C's customers, which the lowest on-time rate of 0.98 suggests.
The added road violations do not create safety risks that matter more than on-time delivery.
B and C will keep operating normally rather than changing strategy after being overridden.

unknowns: How B and C will respond to being overridden, for example by changing routing or parking behaviour, or by voting against later amendments.
Why C loses so much utility, and whether a smaller change or compensation could win C's vote.
How customers perceive the change, beyond the measured on-time figures.
Whether the higher road-violation count carries safety or legal costs that the table does not capture.
Next period's demand and whether the gain holds outside the 5 measured seeds.
Which exact regulation revision (quorum or override clause) would be needed, and what precedent it sets for future votes.
